text:
**For a full recharge in one day of good sun, plan on about 300 W of panels. If you can wait a day and a half, 200 W is enough.**

**The math**

Panel watts ≈ 1,000 Wh ÷ (peak sun hours × ~0.7 to 0.75 for real-world losses)

| Conditions | Peak sun hours | Panel watts for a one-day recharge |
|---|---|---|
| Winter or cloudy | 2-3 | ~450-735 W |
| Average US day | 4-4.5 | ~320-340 W |
| Good summer day | 5-6 | ~230-300 W |

Sources: [Power Station Runtime](https://power-runtime.pages.dev/guides/solar-charging/) and [Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/).

**If you'd rather go smaller**

- A 200 W panel makes about 600-630 Wh on an average day, so a 1,000 Wh station fills in roughly 1.5 days ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/), [Watt48](https://www.watt48.com/guides/solar-panel-charging-power-station)).
- A quick rule of thumb is battery Wh ÷ 5, which gives about 200 W.
- A 400 W panel would recharge in under a day, with margin for clouds.

**Check before you buy**

1. **Your station's maximum solar input in watts.** Anything above it is wasted. Many 1,000 Wh units accept 400-800 W, but some cap at 200 W ([Held in Reserve](https://www.heldinreserve.com/power/solar-panels-recharge-power-station/)).
2. **Its input voltage range versus the panel's open-circuit voltage (Voc).** Exceeding the limit can damage the station, especially when you wire panels in series ([Power Preflight](https://powerpreflight.com/guides/solar-panel-sizing-portable-power-stations/)).
3. **Whether you'll run devices while charging.** Your load subtracts from the solar input, so recharging takes longer.
4. **Aiming the panel.** Tilting it toward the sun and adjusting a few times a day can add 20-30%.

**A 400 W option**

The [ALLPOWERS SP037 400 W foldable panel](https://dealectric.com/go/allpowers-sp037-400w-solar-panel) is listed at $299, or $269.10 with code ALLPOWERS26, which expires 2026-12-30. Its Voc is 45.3 V, which suits 12-60 V solar inputs, and it comes with MC4-to-XT60 and DC adapters. It weighs 18.5 kg (about 41 lb), which is heavy for a folding panel. It's too high-voltage for stations with low input windows, such as the Tenergy T320 and BLUETTI Elite 30 V2. If your station caps solar input below 400 W, a smaller panel makes more sense.
